title: the commandment about rest, which is the one everybody breaks
hook: the commandment about rest, which is the one everybody breaks

segments.voice: Yesterday, the last line of the Lord's Prayer: deliver us. A prayer that ends by asking for help. Your line was: you can ask. Did you ask for anything? Day nine.

Quick test. Name a day in the last month when you did no work at all. No email, no errands, no catching up on the laundry. Not a sick day. A day you stopped on purpose. Most people can't. And most people, asked about the Ten Commandments, would say they're doing fine. No stealing, no murder, a decent record overall. But one of the ten is about rest. It's longer than the one about murder. And it's the one almost everybody breaks, every single week, and brags about it. Today's word is that commandment.
screen: `NAME ONE DAY YOU STOPPED.` → `ONE OF THE TEN IS ABOUT REST.` → `THE ONE EVERYBODY BREAKS.`

segments.voice: The Sabbath. In Hebrew, shabbat, from a root that means to stop. To cease. Not to relax, exactly. To stop. Here's the commandment, in the book of Exodus, in the old King James Bible: "Remember the sabbath day, to keep it holy. Six days shalt thou labour, and do all thy work." Then the seventh day is set apart. No work. And then the text does something surprising. It makes a list of who gets to rest. You, and your son and your daughter. Your servants. Your animals. Even the stranger staying in your town. Nobody is left out. The boss can't rest while the workers keep going. In a world where most people worked every day they were able, that was radical. One day in seven, everybody puts it down. The reason Exodus gives goes back to the first page of the Bible: God made the world in six days and rested on the seventh. Rest isn't laziness. It's part of the pattern of creation. Now, Christians keep this in different ways, and it's worth knowing who does what. Jews keep the Sabbath on Saturday, from sundown Friday, and Jesus, as a Jew, kept it too. Most Christians made Sunday their holy day, because it's the day they celebrate Jesus rising from the dead, and many call it the Lord's Day. Some Christians, like Seventh-day Adventists, keep Saturday. Different days, the same commandment. And then there's a moment in Mark's Gospel. Jesus's friends are walking through a field on the Sabbath, picking grain because they're hungry, and some religious teachers object. Jesus answers: "The sabbath was made for man, and not man for the sabbath." Jewish teachers said something very close to that too. The day is a gift, not a trap. Which means stopping isn't something you earn after the work is done. It's the gift itself.
screen: `SHABBAT — TO STOP.` · `EVERYBODY RESTS, EVEN THE STRANGER.` · `SATURDAY, SUNDAY: ONE COMMANDMENT.` · `MADE FOR PEOPLE, NOT PEOPLE FOR IT.` · then, large: `STOPPING IS THE GIFT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice, and it's the simplest one yet. Stop. Put the phone face down, or leave it where it is and take your hand off it. Let your shoulders drop. Don't plan the rest of the day. Don't review what you didn't finish. For forty-five seconds, nothing is required of you. If you pray, you can offer the stillness as a small Sabbath. If you don't, just notice what it feels like when nobody needs anything from you. The bell holds the time.
The Sabbath. Shabbat. A day to stop, made for people, given to everyone. Ninth word.
Your line: stop. it counts. Once today, stop in the middle of something for one full minute, and don't feel guilty about it. That minute isn't wasted. Day nine.

howItsDone: Most Christians set Sunday apart as the Lord's Day, with worship and, for many, a day of rest; some, like Seventh-day Adventists, keep the Sabbath on Saturday. Jews keep Shabbat from sundown Friday to Saturday night.

original.note: Hebrew. from a root meaning to stop or cease. English "sabbath" comes from it, through Greek and Latin.

trapdoor: what you thought: an old rule about not working on Sundays.
what it means: shabbat, to stop. one day in seven when everybody, servants and strangers included, puts the work down.
what a scholar hears: Exodus grounds it in creation, God resting on the seventh day, and Deuteronomy's version grounds it in freedom from slavery in Egypt. two reasons, one day.

notes: 'Jewish teachers said something very close' refers to the Mekhilta on Exodus 31:13 (attributed to R. Shimon ben Menasya: the Sabbath is given to you, not you to the Sabbath). Included so the Mark 2 scene doesn't read as a verdict on Judaism; confirm.
Hook claims the Sabbath commandment is longer than the one about murder (Exodus 20:8–11 vs 20:13): true in any translation, but confirm tone.
Sunday as the Lord's Day and Saturday-keeping churches (Seventh-day Adventists, Seventh Day Baptists) stated simply; confirm the Keeper is happy naming Adventists.
'In a world where most people worked every day they were able' is a general historical statement; soften if needed.
Trapdoor mentions Deuteronomy 5:15's reason (remember you were a servant in Egypt), not taught in the voice; it is a 'go deeper' detail.
